messages.subject: Re: Does Distance underestimate transect area?
messages.subject_clean: Does Distance underestimate transect area?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Florian, list,

Strictly speaking, when you are doing a line transect you must ignore=20
all observations "outside" the rectangle that you refer to, defined by=20
the transect.

And note that the problem is not just about the way the transect area is=20
calculated, but also a more subtle yet equally important one. If you=20
consider data from the "hemispherical cap" you refer to, an half circle=20
at each end of the transects, then you are mixing data from line=20
transects and point transects - your transect becomes in fact a line=20
transect + a point transect (1 half of a point transect at each end).=20
The analysis of such data is not possible using conventional methods,=20
because now you do not know what is the underlying distribution of=20
distances is (which is assumed uniform for lines and triangular for=20
points in the conventional setting, which is typically guaranteed by=20
placing many samplers - lines or points - using a random design=20
independent of animal distribution).

So, in short, you need to ignore the data "outside" the rectangular=20
transect. In most situations, with large areas, this is not an issue and=20
simple to do. A more complicated approach, if your half circles are so=20
large that a good proportion of the data comes from them, is to change=20
your design to points rather than lines, or (which for simplicity I=20
would try to avoid) to do both but then extra care must be used to=20
ensure independence of the two source of data, which would be analyzed=20
separately.

Cheers

Tiago

Dear All=20

I have a question regarding goodness of fit diagnostic tests incorporated=
 in DISTANCE 5.0. I am trying to compare the suitability of several model=
s to estimates the detection function. I know that the AIC is the measure=
 to check for this purpose but I also wanted to see the information provi=
ded by the other diagnostics. I have consulted the DISTANCE manual but un=
fortunately I couldnt find the answer there. My question is" If I am retu=
rned with the calculated values of D_n, W-sq and C-sq, where are the tabu=
lated values for these statistics that I should check against for either =
to accept or to reject the null hypothesis of the model being conforming =
to the data or otherwise?"=20

Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
-----------------------

D_n =3D 0.1771 p =3D 0.0049

Cramer-von Mises family tests
-----------------------------

W-sq (uniform weighting) =3D 0.2342 0.200 < p <=3D 0.300
Relevant critical values:

W-sq crit(alpha=3D0.300) =3D 0.1837
W-sq crit(alpha=3D0.200) =3D 0.2406

C-sq (cosine weighting) =3D 0.2120 0.100 < p <=3D 0.150
Relevant critical values:
C-sq crit(alpha=3D0.150) =3D 0.1910
C-sq crit(alpha=3D0.100) =3D 0.2352

I can see that I have a low p value in K-S test indicating high significa=
nce but for D_n value I cant check it against a tabulated value. The seco=
nd thing is the alpha value in the Cramer -von Mises test is selected in =
a diffeferent level for different models I am using so how can I fix the =
alpha level for all my computations to render the test statistic comparab=
le across all model evaluations?=20

I hope that is not a sillly question and regards to you all.

----------------------------------------
Husam El Alqamy, B.Sc., M.Phil.

Terrestrial Environmental Research Center, TERC
Environmental Agency Abu Dhabi

messages.subject_clean: Cremer von-Mises interpratation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hussam, list

I think you have all the information you need in the output, but perhaps
it is not explained as clearly as it should be.

The p-value quoted is the probability with which you would expect a fit
this bad, or worse, if the model were correct.  If the p-value is low,
that is evidence that the model is unlikely to have generated those
data, so that the model is not a good fit to the data.  We often use a
critical value (alpha level) of 0.05 in hypothesis testing, so a value
of 0.05 or less means "reject the model".  I'm not so rigid as that,
usually -- instead a low p (say 0.15 or less) is one signal telling me
to look and see where the model is not fitting the data well.

In your case, for the KS test, you have a p of 0.0049, so strong
evidence for a lack of fit.  The KS test uses only the largest departure
between model and data, so in theory is less powerful than the CvM tests.

Unlike the KS test output, the CvM tests do not give a p value to 4
decimal places, for a technical reason (we can't work them out).
Instead, it tells you what range the p value falls between.  For the
uniform weighting, it falls between 0.2 and 0.3.  For the cosine
weighting (which gives more weight to data close to 0 distance) it falls
between 0.1 and 0.15.  The fact that the cosine weighting gives a lower
p value tells me that your lack of fit is worse at smaller distances.
In general, unlike the KS test, the CvM test looks at all the departures
between model and data, not just the largest one.  The fact the the KS
test has a very low p but the CvMs don't tells me that you have a
problem at just a restricted range of distances, rather than a general
problem with fit.  My guess is that you maybe have a problem with too
many zero distances -- or perhaps serious rounding at smaller distances?
  The qq-plot (and detection function plots) will tell you.

In terms of reporting results in a paper I tend to use the KS test
because (a) it gives exact p values, and (b) although it's supposed to
be less powerful, in practice they usually give about the same answer
(although in your case they don't).  Outside of reporting things in
papers, however, they do tell you slightly different things so it's
worth looking at them all and understanding what they tell you.

You mentioned the alpha levels given in the CvM test output.  Let's take
an example:

> > W-sq (uniform weighting) = 0.2342 0.200 < p <= 0.300
> > Relevant critical values:
> > W-sq crit(alpha=0.300) = 0.1837
> > W-sq crit(alpha=0.200) = 0.2406

What this is saying is that the test statistic value (the W-sq) was
0.2342, which means the corresponding p-value was between 0.2 and 0.3.
It then gives the value of W-sq that corresponds with the p-values of
0.2 and 0.3 (ie alpha of 0.2 and 0.3) - in this case if the W-sq value
had been 0.1837 the p value would have been exactly 0.3, and if the W-sq
value had been 0.2406 the p-value would have been exactly 0.2.  If the
p-value had been between, say 0.1 and 0.2, it would have given those
critical W-sq values.  I think it brackets the p value to the nearest
0.1 until it gets down to p=0.1 below which it brackets things more
precisely (can't remember the actual boundaries offhand).

Hope this helps,

  - len

--

Magaly, it is a judgement call which you do.  The problem with missing
effort is that it isn't missing at random.  If you assume it is, then
you just reduce the line length and proceed as normal.  If the missing
effort might be correlated with animal density, then you would want to
exclude the region that effort represents from your study area, as it
was unsurveyed.  You then estimate density and abundance for the
remaining area.  In this case, it is difficult sometimes to say what
part of your intended study area corresponds to the missing effort.
With a parallel line design, the easy way to define it is to say that it
extends halfway to the next line.  If you only delete the area in the
strip, then you again end up with unbalanced survey area through your
study region, and if the density around the missing strips is not
average, then you will get bias.

Conceptually, I don't think there is any difference between effort
missing through fog and effort missing through technical problems,
except perhaps in scale.  If fog caused you to miss only short sections
of line, and affected only a small percentage of total effort, then the
first solution of just shortening your lines appropriately makes sense.
If the technical problem caused you to miss an extensive part of your
study area, then the only sensible option is to reduce your study area
to the area where you do have data - i.e. the second solution.

Steve Buckland

Dear list,

I have been working on some DISTANCE analysis and have encountered some problems
with interpretation of my results.  I am confused about what I think I have
done correctly but a reviewer of my paper has identified as non-convergence
issue of my models.  (if the reviewer recognizes this paper/problem, I would be
happy to discuss with you privately or am also fine if you prefer to remain
anonymous through the listserve).

I used MCDS to assess seabird detectability from vessel surveys and looked at
several covariates (Year, Observer, SeaState, etc.) which might affect
detectability of each species.

In my results, I compare different models, for example: Null model (no
covariates), model with Year covariate, model with Year and Observer
covariates, etc.  The deltaAICc scores the models range from 0 to over 10.
>From all of my experience with AIC and from Burnham and Anderson, I find this
spread of scores is very typical.  In each of my analyses, the Results tab do
indeed say that ?Convergence was achieved with 6 function evaluations? or
some other number of evaluations.

The problem:  The reviewer of my paper has suggests that many of my models did
not converge and they can tell because deltaAICc of nested models should never
be greater than twice the difference in the number of parameter.  The reviewer
suggests to start with the simplest model and add covariates while setting the
initial values of the parameter estimates from the previous model.  This is
described on pg. 119 of Distance user guide as a ?stepwise? model
selection.

Questions:

1)	Is this forward ?stepwise? approach the same as building ?nested?
models?  Why must I use this complicated approach to model building?
2)	If my not ?nested? models DO converge (as indicated by the output
results), why can I not simply compare the deltaAICc scores of these
independent models?  AIC theory encourages you to decide on a set of a priori
models to compare and rank rather than building with a stepwise approach.
DISTANCE program seems better suited to the former (set of a priori models)
rather than the latter approach (stepwise model building).

Thanks for your help.  I welcome feedback from anyone.

Rob

messages.body_plain:
Rob, I was not the reviewer, but the comments make a lot of sense.  If
you add a single parameter to a model, then AIC can at most increase by
2.  However, if you add a factor-type covariate to a model, you're
adding say m-1 parameters, where m is the number of levels of that
factor (e.g. m=5 observers).  Then the maximum difference in AIC that
you can get is 2*(m-1).  If you have increases greater than this, then
convergence has not occurred.

The approach suggested by the reviewer is sensible, and is not
complicated;  this is easily done in Distance.  The forwards stepwise
approach is just one way of selecting between nested models, and the
easiest.

Your models are not 'independent' - they share common parameters.  You
can if you want look at all the possible models, with and without each
of the possible covariates, but this will be a much more laborious task
than the approach suggested by the reviewer.  You can't simply look at
models with a single covariate, to decide which covariates to include.
You also need to look at the models which include any 2, any 3, any 4,
... of your potential covariates.  Or you can choose an arbitrary subset
of these models, and risk missing a much better model.

Steve Buckland

Robert, your models ARE nested.  It doesn't matter whether you use
Distance or not, you have a model selection problem, with nested
models.  Forwards stepping doesn't guarantee that you get to the best
model, nor does your strategy.  Whether your model fits have converged
or not is another issue.  You may have tried the best model, but failed
to fit it, so falsely reject it, with your approach.  The reviewer's
suggestion is a strategy to avoid that problem.  It is also a sensible
strategy for selecting a good model (not necessarily the best model)
even when there are no convergence issues.  That strategy will still be
good if you need more than 2 covariates in your model.  Your strategy
becomes unwieldy if you have a number of potential covariates -
especially if you consider models with more than 2 covariates.

Steve Buckland

Robert, your models ARE nested.  It doesn't matter whether you use
Distance or not, you have a model selection problem, with nested
models.  Forwards stepping doesn't guarantee that you get to the best
model, nor does your strategy.  Whether your model fits have converged
or not is another issue.  You may have tried the best model, but failed
to fit it, so falsely reject it, with your approach.  The reviewer's
suggestion is a strategy to avoid that problem.  It is also a sensible
strategy for selecting a good model (not necessarily the best model)
even when there are no convergence issues.  That strategy will still be
good if you need more than 2 covariates in your model.  Your strategy
becomes unwieldy if you have a number of potential covariates -
especially if you consider models with more than 2 covariates.

Steve Buckland

Hi,
I am little bit puzzled by the discussion and suggestion to stick with a
template, stepwise approach as such. To me, the real issue is eventually
the effect on the final densities (is there, how severe, and is it for
real/generalizable ?).

I remember many discussions arguing against stepwiseAIC.
Here a good reference on the issue:

Why do we still use stepwise modelling in ecology and behaviour?
MARK J. WHITTINGHAM, PHILIP A. STEPHENS, RICHARD B. BRADBURY and ROBERT P.
FRECKLETON
Journal of Animal Ecology (2006) 75, 1182=961189
doi: 10.1111/j.1365-2656.2006.01141.x
ABSTRACT
    * 1.
      The biases and shortcomings of stepwise multiple regression are wel=
l
established within the statistical literature. However, an
examination of papers published in 2004 by three leading ecological
and behavioural journals suggested that the use of this technique
remains widespread: of 65 papers in which a multiple regression
approach was used, 57% of studies used a stepwise procedure.
    * 2.
      The principal drawbacks of stepwise multiple regression include bia=
s
in parameter estimation, inconsistencies among model selection
algorithms, an inherent (but often overlooked) problem of multiple
hypothesis testing, and an inappropriate focus or reliance on a
single best model. We discuss each of these issues with examples.
    * 3.
      We use a worked example of data on yellowhammer distribution
collected over 4 years to highlight the pitfalls of stepwise
regression. We show that stepwise regression allows models
containing significant predictors to be obtained from each year's
data. In spite of the significance of the selected models, they vary
substantially between years and suggest patterns that are at odds
with those determined by analysing the full, 4-year data set.
    * 4.
      An information theoretic (IT) analysis of the yellowhammer data set
illustrates why the varying outcomes of stepwise analyses arise. In
particular, the IT approach identifies large numbers of competing
models that could describe the data equally well, showing that no
one model should be relied upon for inference.

Perhaps somebody has more insights on this in the context of DS,
densities, covariates and (non-linear) higher order interactions.
Thanks; very best
  Falk

Falk, it is pragmatic. If you have convergence problems, it is a way to=20
overcome these. And looking at all possible models is not pragmatic -=20
because the number can be huge if you have a number of potential=20
covariates, and because failure to converge will dog many of the model=20
fits. Yes, if you can do all possible models, and you can coax Distance=20
to converge by playing around with starting values, then I would favour=20
that strategy, together with use of e.g. AIC weights. Stepwise doesn't=20
guarantee that you end up with the right model - but then no procedure=20
does, even if there is a right model out there to be found. It is likely=20
though to lead you to a model that generates good abundance estimates -=20
provided you have good data.

In fact, there is another reason why people typically don't use a=20
model-averaging approach in distance sampling. With good data, you tend=20
to see very similar estimates from different models, so you gain little=20
from model-averaging. In Distance, if you were to use model averaging=20
with say AIC weights, you would have to extract results from Distance=20
and do this externally. However, you can bootstrap, with several models=20
selected, and Distance will use AIC (or AICc or BIC) to select the best=20
model for each resample, and the average of the bootstrap estimates of=20
any parameter of interest (e.g. abundance) will then be a model-averaged=20
estimate.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Supplementing what Steve said, model convergence and model selection are=20
NOT the same things. Also, just because an optimization routine says it=20
converged doesn't mean that it converged to the MLE. Routines can be=20
fooled by flat spots on the likelihood surface. It is incumbent on the=20
user to make sure the results make sense. One thing a user can easily=20
check is to compare models that are nested which means that one model=20
contains all of the same parameters of a simpler model (and more).=20
Anytime you add parameters to a model, the likelihood should improve or=20
stay the same (negative likelihood will get smaller). This is the same=20
as adding variables in a multiple regression. In that case the R-squared=20
will always get higher. That is why model selection criteria always=20
contain a penalty for the number of fitted parameters. If there was no=20
penalty the criterion (eg, log-likelihood, R-squared) would always=20
improve unless the optimization didn't converge at the true parameters.=20
One way to help the optimization code (if there is a problem) is to set=20
the starting values at the values from the simpler model and set the=20
values for the new parameters to 0. That should provide the exact same=20
likelihood value as the simpler model and then the optimization code can=20
start from that point. This is a method of improving convergence (if=20
there is a problem) and NOT a prescribed method for model selection. If=20
you have 2 nested models with the larger model containing the parameters=20
of the simpler model and k more parameters, the delta AIC=3DAIC for=20
complex model - AIC for simpler model, should not exceed 2k because the=20
difference in the -2Lnl should <0 (ie the negative log-likelihood for=20
the larger model should be smaller than the neg log-likelihood of the=20
simpler model). This only works if the models are nested. A simple model=20
with cluster size and a more complex model with cluster size and=20
beaufort are nested. But 2 models, one with cluster size and the other=20
with beaufort are not nested. AIC works for both nested and non-nested=20
models but when you have nested models comparing AIC (or log-likelihood=20
values) provides a check on the optimization code.

--jeff

This discussion was informative and for seeing implementations and
philosophies followed (of which there are several).

If I understood it correctly, it looks like the term 'converged' is not that
clear then in the current DS software.

On the future vision topic:

If allowed to express here, myself, I favor concepts brought forward by
Breiman (2001)

Breiman, L. 2001. Statistical modeling: the two cultures. Statistical
Science. 16(3): 199 -	231.

With that, most of the discussions and uncertainties would basically go away
by itself, e.g. stepwise model selection, AIC, thresholds, nestedness, model
fits, linearity.

I am aware that currently neither DS, nor CMR, are using such algorithms in
their software implementations. But it really should be done, and can be
achieved quite easily in R and others.

Something for the (near) future.

I would predict that such methods like boosting and bagging will play an
increasingly big role in our discipline very soon.

I am also fully aware that thou shall not be married to just one
algorithm/method alone... (statistical monogamy is probably harmful here).

Supplementing what Steve said, model convergence and model selection are
NOT the same things. Also, just because an optimization routine says it
converged doesn't mean that it converged to the MLE. Routines can be
fooled by flat spots on the likelihood surface. It is incumbent on the
user to make sure the results make sense. One thing a user can easily
check is to compare models that are nested which means that one model
contains all of the same parameters of a simpler model (and more).
Anytime you add parameters to a model, the likelihood should improve or
stay the same (negative likelihood will get smaller). This is the same
as adding variables in a multiple regression. In that case the R-squared
will always get higher. That is why model selection criteria always
contain a penalty for the number of fitted parameters. If there was no
penalty the criterion (eg, log-likelihood, R-squared) would always
improve unless the optimization didn't converge at the true parameters.
One way to help the optimization code (if there is a problem) is to set
the starting values at the values from the simpler model and set the
values for the new parameters to 0. That should provide the exact same
likelihood value as the simpler model and then the optimization code can
start from that point. This is a method of improving convergence (if
there is a problem) and NOT a prescribed method for model selection. If
you have 2 nested models with the larger model containing the parameters
of the simpler model and k more parameters, the delta AIC=AIC for
complex model - AIC for simpler model, should not exceed 2k because the
difference in the -2Lnl should <0 (ie the negative log-likelihood for
the larger model should be smaller than the neg log-likelihood of the
simpler model). This only works if the models are nested. A simple model
with cluster size and a more complex model with cluster size and
beaufort are nested. But 2 models, one with cluster size and the other
with beaufort are not nested. AIC works for both nested and non-nested
models but when you have nested models comparing AIC (or log-likelihood
values) provides a check on the optimization code.

--jeff

Hi,

thanks.
This discussion was informative and for seeing implementations and
philosophies followed (of which there are several).

If I understood it correctly, it looks like the term 'converged' is not that
clear then in the current DS software.

On the future vision topic:

If allowed to express here, myself, I favor concepts brought forward by
Breiman (2001)

Breiman, L. 2001. Statistical modeling: the two cultures. Statistical
Science. 16(3): 199 -	231.

With that, most of the discussions and uncertainties would basically go away
by itself, e.g. stepwise model selection, AIC, thresholds, nestedness, model
fits, linearity.

I am aware that currently neither DS, nor CMR, are using such algorithms in
their software implementations. But it really should be done, and can be
achieved quite easily in R and others.

Something for the (near) future.

I would predict that such methods like boosting and bagging will play an
increasingly big role in our discipline very soon.

I am also fully aware that thou shall not be married to just one
algorithm/method alone... (statistical monogamy is probably harmful here).

Very best

Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] stepwise AIC ? Re: [DIST-SAMP] Model convergence,
nested models, and interpretation of AIC results

Supplementing what Steve said, model convergence and model selection are
NOT the same things. Also, just because an optimization routine says it
converged doesn't mean that it converged to the MLE. Routines can be
fooled by flat spots on the likelihood surface. It is incumbent on the
user to make sure the results make sense. One thing a user can easily
check is to compare models that are nested which means that one model
contains all of the same parameters of a simpler model (and more).
Anytime you add parameters to a model, the likelihood should improve or
stay the same (negative likelihood will get smaller). This is the same
as adding variables in a multiple regression. In that case the R-squared
will always get higher. That is why model selection criteria always
contain a penalty for the number of fitted parameters. If there was no
penalty the criterion (eg, log-likelihood, R-squared) would always
improve unless the optimization didn't converge at the true parameters.
One way to help the optimization code (if there is a problem) is to set
the starting values at the values from the simpler model and set the
values for the new parameters to 0. That should provide the exact same
likelihood value as the simpler model and then the optimization code can
start from that point. This is a method of improving convergence (if
there is a problem) and NOT a prescribed method for model selection. If
you have 2 nested models with the larger model containing the parameters
of the simpler model and k more parameters, the delta AIC=AIC for
complex model - AIC for simpler model, should not exceed 2k because the
difference in the -2Lnl should <0 (ie the negative log-likelihood for
the larger model should be smaller than the neg log-likelihood of the
simpler model). This only works if the models are nested. A simple model
with cluster size and a more complex model with cluster size and
beaufort are nested. But 2 models, one with cluster size and the other
with beaufort are not nested. AIC works for both nested and non-nested
models but when you have nested models comparing AIC (or log-likelihood
values) provides a check on the optimization code.

--jeff

> > Supplementing what Steve said, model convergence and model selection are
> > NOT the same things. Also, just because an optimization routine says it
> > converged doesn't mean that it converged to the MLE. Routines can be
> > fooled by flat spots on the likelihood surface. It is incumbent on the
> > user to make sure the results make sense. One thing a user can easily
> > check is to compare models that are nested which means that one model
> > contains all of the same parameters of a simpler model (and more).
> > Anytime you add parameters to a model, the likelihood should improve or
> > stay the same (negative likelihood will get smaller). This is the same
> > as adding variables in a multiple regression. In that case the R-squared
> > will always get higher. That is why model selection criteria always
> > contain a penalty for the number of fitted parameters. If there was no
> > penalty the criterion (eg, log-likelihood, R-squared) would always
> > improve unless the optimization didn't converge at the true parameters.
> > One way to help the optimization code (if there is a problem) is to set
> > the starting values at the values from the simpler model and set the
> > values for the new parameters to 0. That should provide the exact same
> > likelihood value as the simpler model and then the optimization code can
> > start from that point. This is a method of improving convergence (if
> > there is a problem) and NOT a prescribed method for model selection. If
> > you have 2 nested models with the larger model containing the parameters
> > of the simpler model and k more parameters, the delta AIC=AIC for
> > complex model - AIC for simpler model, should not exceed 2k because the
> > difference in the -2Lnl should <0 (ie the negative log-likelihood for
> > the larger model should be smaller than the neg log-likelihood of the
> > simpler model). This only works if the models are nested. A simple model
> > with cluster size and a more complex model with cluster size and
> > beaufort are nested. But 2 models, one with cluster size and the other
> > with beaufort are not nested. AIC works for both nested and non-nested
> > models but when you have nested models comparing AIC (or log-likelihood
> > values) provides a check on the optimization code.
> >
> > --jeff

There is also a Biometrics paper, Melville and Welsh:

Melville, G. J. and Welsh, A. H. (2001). Line transect sampling in small
regions. Bio-
metrics 57, 1130-1137.

Biometrics allowed us to respond - the authors' response to our response
has a couple of rather silly errors!  Our response is at

Fewster, R.M., Laake, J.L. and Buckland, S.T. 2005.  Line transect
sampling in small and large regions.  /Biometrics/ *61*, 856-859.

Series B wouldn't contemplate publishing any response - so not even the
mathematical errors in Barry and Welsh have been corrected!  However,
the following articles are relevant:

Fewster, R.M. and Buckland, S.T. 2004.  Assessment of distance sampling
estimators.  In /Advanced Distance Sampling/, pp281-306.  S.T. Buckland,
D.R. Anderson, K.P. Burnham, J.L. Laake, D.L. Borchers and L. Thomas
(eds).  Oxford University Press, Oxford.

Fewster, R.M., Southwell, C., Borchers, D.L., Buckland, S.T. and Pople,
A.R. 2008.  The influence of animal mobility on the assumption of
uniform distances in aerial line transect surveys.  /Wildlife Research/
*35*, 275-288.

Fewster, R.M., Buckland, S.T., Burnham, K.P., Borchers, D.L., Jupp,
P.E., Laake, J.L. and Thomas, L. in press.  Estimating the encounter
rate variance in distance sampling.  /Biometrics/.

The ANZJS article was so over the top, it didn't merit any response!

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: baffling problem with mean cluster size calculations in Distance
messages.body_plain:
well, at least it remains baffling to me after a couple days trying to
resolve it (and searching the discussion board archives).

Context:
- aerial surveys of moose, line transect sampling, stratified design.
- due to limited encounter rate in each strata, want to use global
estimate of cluster size.
- in order to match past analyses, estimate cluster size as average across
just those clusters detected within 200m of transect.

Bafflement:
Cluster Size / Global Estimates
Effort        :    1765.563
 # samples     :   132
 Width         :    155.0000    #NOTE: 200-blind strip width
 # observations:    43
 Expected cluster size estimated as average of cluster size measurements.
 Mean cluster size     =  0.72093     Standard error    =  0.20194

(i) all clusters of moose contain at least 1 moose, so mean cluster size
should be > 1
(and  the 'Cluster Size' values of the observation layer are all > = 1);
(ii) data layers appear to have been imported correctly, including
'Cluster Size' field;
(iii) doing this calculation in R, the 43 observations give:
         a mean size of 1.7209 (= Distance estimate +1, but perhaps I'm
being paranoid),
        SE              0.1318  (!= 0.20194).

Clearly something is wrong somewhere, presumably in what I'm asking
DISTANCE to do.
ANY SUGGESTIONS?

some other relevant summaries to demonstrate I've checked the obvious (to
me) possible sources:

(from Estimation Options)
Parameter Estimation Specification
 ----------------------------------
 Encounter rate by stratum
 Detection probability for all data combined
 Expected cluster size for all data combined
 Density by stratum
 Pooled estimate of density is made from area weighted stratum estimates

...
Clusters:
 ---------
 Analysis based on exact sizes
 Include s(i) only if x(i) <=   155.0000
 Expected value of cluster size computed by: simple average
...

####
I'm happy to consolidate any replies for a summary post to the list.

Cheers,
Joel

I am experiencing some difficulties in manually calculating effective
strip widths for selected covariate levels in a MCDS analysis. I think my
methods follow exactly the directions given in the online help, yet the
results don't seem to fit.

now I've come upon one where my constructed estimates are not even in the
ballpark of the program's ESW estimate, which makes me wonder if I
mishandled the other ones as well.

   Parameter A(1) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.

   Parameter A(2) is the coefficient of level BREED of factor covariate T=
OY.
   Parameter A(3) is the coefficient of level POST of factor covariate TO=

Y.

al

---

     A( 1)      3.917        4.407
     A( 2)     0.3933       0.9132
     A( 3)    -0.3730       0.5553
     A( 4)     0.9323E-02   0.6276E-02

67

####################

This model uses two covariates: factor covariate "TOY" (time of year) wit=

h
three levels winter, breed, and post, and a continuous covariate "minutes
since sunrise".
I want to calculate ESWs for the levels of TOY. My understanding of the
method is: 1) calculate sigma for the particular covariate level, which
would be A(1) for WINTER [3.92], A(1)*exp(A(2)) for BREED [5.8] or

g

I am aware that the number of sightings is on the low side, and so might

g
might be a result of forcing too many parameters on a poor data set size,

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

We perform line transects using a manned submersible to estimate the
density of yelloweye rockfish. We also collect information on other fish
species, such as lingcod, as we perform these transects. We were hoping
to use this same survey to come up with a density estimate of lingcod;
however, these fish seem to have a patchy distribution. They are not in
a school, so I don't know that a cluster analysis is appropriate.
Instead they seem to be normally distributed until there is a patch,
such as a feeding aggregation. We are getting a pretty high variance
estimate due to this patchy distribution. Does anyone have any
suggestions on dealing with this type of data?

Thanks and Happy Halloween!

Jennifer Stahl

Groundfish Fisheries Biologist

Commercial Fisheries Division

Alaska Department of Fish and Game

messages.subject: alternative method of incorporating model selection uncertainty
messages.subject_clean: alternative method of incorporating model selection uncertainty
messages.body_plain:
I would like to get some input on the pros and cons of an alternative met=
hod=20
of incorporating model selection uncertainty into estimates of variance u=
sing=20
bootstrapping in a multiple covariate distance sampling analysis.=20=20

Currently, model averaging is incorporated during the bootstrap option of=
=20
variance estimation.  It works by fitting a set of up to 5 detection func=
tions=20
to the bootstrap sample data at each iteration, and the top model being=20=

selected and used for the abundance estimation for that iteration.  Model=
=20
selection uncertainty is thereby included in the width of the ensuing=20
confidence intervals calculated from the bootstrap estimates.

My alternative method differs by using a single set of best models, selec=
ted=20
from the original data, to compute a model-average estimate at each=20
iteration.  In other words, I first use the original data to select a set=
 of best=20
models to use for estimation.  Then, at each iteration of the bootstrap I=
=20
compute the model average estimate of abundance based on this set of=20
models and associated parameter estimates.  The model average estimate is=
=20
the average of estimates weighted by model weight.  The bootstrap=20
abundance estimate and 95% confidence limits are then calculated as usual=
.

An analyst might prefer this method for 2 reasons: 1) For some data (e.g.=
=20
sparse data) there will likely be convergence problems that will go undet=
ected=20
in some (perhaps many) iterations during the automated model selection=20=

occurring in each bootstrap iteration.  2) It is computationally challeng=
ing to=20
have to re-fit a set of detection functions at each iteration, especially=
 when=20
covariates differ across models in multiple covariate distance sampling.

The basic question is: "does my proposed method adequately incorporate=20=

model selection uncertainty, given the constraints I mention?"

messages.body_plain:
I would like to get some input on the pros and cons of an alternative met=
hod=20
of incorporating model selection uncertainty into estimates of variance u=
sing=20
bootstrapping in a multiple covariate distance sampling analysis.=20=20

Currently, model averaging is incorporated during the bootstrap option of=
=20
variance estimation.  It works by fitting a set of up to 5 detection func=
tions=20
to the bootstrap sample data at each iteration, and the top model being=20=

selected and used for the abundance estimation for that iteration.  Model=
=20
selection uncertainty is thereby included in the width of the ensuing=20
confidence intervals calculated from the bootstrap estimates.

My alternative method differs by using a single set of best models, selec=
ted=20
from the original data, to compute a model-average estimate at each=20
iteration.  In other words, I first use the original data to select a set=
 of best=20
models to use for estimation.  Then, at each iteration of the bootstrap I=
=20
compute the model average estimate of abundance based on this set of=20
models and associated parameter estimates.  The model average estimate is=
=20
the average of estimates weighted by model weight.  The bootstrap=20
abundance estimate and 95% confidence limits are then calculated as usual=
.

An analyst might prefer this method for 2 reasons: 1) For some data (e.g.=
=20
sparse data) there will likely be convergence problems that will go undet=
ected=20
in some (perhaps many) iterations during the automated model selection=20=

occurring in each bootstrap iteration.  2) It is computationally challeng=
ing to=20
have to re-fit a set of detection functions at each iteration, especially=
 when=20
covariates differ across models in multiple covariate distance sampling.

The basic question is: "does my proposed method adequately incorporate=20=

model selection uncertainty, given the constraints I mention?"

o look=20
for the succession of birds after farm abandonment. I am comparing each=20=

species distribution in habitat at different succession stage. I did poin=
t survey.=20
Now when I am analyzing my data, I found a problem with some bird species=
,=20
such as common yellow throat warblers and grey catbirds, were attracted t=
o=20
the observer (me). Their data showed a sharp peak at distance within 5=20=

meters from the observer. The detection function fits poorly (p=3D0.0000)=
 and=20
the output is way too large (56 birds/hectare).

I think this problem was mentioned in Buckland et al., 2001, but there di=
dn't=20
seem to be a standard solution. I tried to left truncate my data, which l=
argely=20
reduced the density estimation while slightly improved the detection func=
tion=20
fitness. I don't think left-truncation is the way to handle the problem b=
ecause=20
it removed a lot of the observation which, even though biased, should act=
ually=20
be there.

What I just did now was I added 2 meters to all of my observation of this=
=20
species. In another word, I "artificially" added two meters to move the c=
urve=20
away from the observer. The output changed from 56birds/ha to 3.2birds/ha=
,=20
which is a reasonable number. And the detection function fitness change f=
rom=20
p=3D0 to p=3D0.30. I also tried to add different distance (1m, 2m, 5m, 10=
m) to the=20
data and not surprisingly, the density estimation reduced as larger dista=
nce=20
was added.=20

I am wondering what you think about this approach to remove the bias caus=
ed=20
by observer's attraction to the birds. It certainly adds an artifact to t=
he=20
observation, but the data fitness and output is more reasonable. And also=
,=20
since my goal is to compare the bird density change among different habit=
at,=20
the absolute number of bird density is not as important as the relative d=
ensity=20
among habitats. But I am still wondering if this is a doable approach. I =
am=20
eager to hear your opinion or suggestions if you have dealt with this kin=
d of=20
bias. Any suggestion would be really appreciated.

Sincerely,
Ai Wen

messages.body_plain:
I think there is a conceptual difference between the two strategies.  In
the first, you're allowing any of the possible models to be the 'true'
model, and you're quantifying the variation arising from using different
models supported by the data.  With your proposed approach, you're
essentially saying that the 'true' model is an average of the selected
models, and you're using the bootstrap to quantify uncertainty arising
from having to estimate the weights.  I would expect this approach to
yield smaller variances, and not really to quantify model uncertainty
appropriately.

Steve Buckland
